title: Math is Playful
contentObjective: I can use patterns and relationships to make sense of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle and think logically about its solutions.
languageObjective: I can describe a puzzle strategy using the words pattern, rule, and predict.

noticeAndWonder.context: Three rods stand on a wooden base. On the left rod, a stack of discs is arranged with the smallest on top and the largest on the bottom.
noticeStarters: I notice the number of rods is ___ .
I notice the discs are stacked ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder what happens if you add ___ .
noticeAndWonder.imageAlt: Four Rubik's cubes in different states of being solved.

turnAndTalk.question: A one-disc Tower of Hanoi takes 1 move, a two-disc tower takes 3 moves, and a three-disc tower takes 7 moves. What pattern rule takes you from one row to the next?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The pattern rule is to double the previous number of moves and add 1: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3, and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7.

stems.en: The pattern rule is to ___ the number of moves and then ___.
stems.es: La regla del patrón es ___ el número de movimientos y luego ___.

stems.en: I know the rule works because ___.
stems.es: Sé que la regla funciona porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer states 'double and add 1' and checks it against both jumps (1→3 and 3→7). A weak answer only notices the numbers are growing without naming the rule.
turnAndTalk.extend: Using the pattern rule, predict the number of moves for a four-disc tower — and justify why you don't need to actually play it out to know your answer is right.
extendStems: A four-disc tower takes ___ moves because 7 × ___ + ___ = ___.
I don't need to play it out because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: When you sorted moves into 'legal move' and 'breaks a rule,' what made 'placing a smaller disc on top of a larger disc' legal but the reverse illegal?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The rule is that a larger disc can never sit on top of a smaller disc — the reverse, smaller on larger, is always allowed.

stems.en: Smaller on larger is legal because ___.
stems.es: Poner el pequeño sobre el grande es legal porque ___.

stems.en: Larger on smaller breaks a rule because ___.
stems.es: Poner el grande sobre el pequeño rompe una regla porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming the size-order rule specifically — a larger disc may never sit on a smaller one — not just 'that one felt wrong.'
turnAndTalk.extend: Someone claims 'moving two discs together in one move' should be allowed because it would make the puzzle faster. Argue against that claim using the actual rules.
extendStems: That move breaks the rule because ___.
Even though it seems faster, it is against the rules because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You know a three-disc tower takes 7 steps. Without playing it, how can the pattern rule tell you the minimum steps for a five-disc tower?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Applying 'double and add 1' twice from 7 gives 15 for four discs, then 31 for five discs.

stems.en: Starting from 7, I apply the rule ___ times to reach ___ steps for five discs.
stems.es: Empezando en 7, aplico la regla ___ veces para llegar a ___ pasos para cinco discos.

stems.en: The pattern lets me predict without playing because ___.
stems.es: El patrón me permite predecir sin jugar porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer shows both steps (7 → 15 → 31) and explains that a pattern rule predicts values you never directly tested. A weak answer just states 31 without showing the doubling steps.
turnAndTalk.extend: Will the number of steps for a Tower of Hanoi puzzle always be odd, no matter how many discs? Justify your answer using the pattern rule.
extendStems: Yes, because doubling any number gives ___, and adding 1 makes it ___.
This will always be true because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, when a problem asked you to organize disc-and-step information, what strategy helped you spot the pattern?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Organizing discs and steps in a table (1→1, 2→3, 3→7, 4→15, 5→31) makes the double-and-add-1 pattern easier to see.

stems.en: I organized the information by ___, which helped me see ___.
stems.es: Organicé la información al ___, lo que me ayudó a ver ___.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy — like building a table — tied to spotting the pattern, not just "I figured it out."
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who doubled the steps but forgot to add 1, getting 14 instead of 15 for four discs? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

vocabulary.definition: A problem designed to be played with — it has rules, a goal, and room to imagine solutions.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un problema diseñado para jugarse: tiene reglas, una meta y espacio para imaginar soluciones.
vocabulary.example: The Tower of Hanoi is a puzzle that was invented in 1883.
vocabulary.visual: Tower of Hanoi: three rods, a stack of discs, and two rules.
vocabulary.cloze: A problem designed to be played with — rules, a goal, room to imagine — is a ___.

examples.why: It has rules, a goal, and many ways in.

examples.text: A page of the same computation twenty times

vocabulary.definition: Something that repeats or changes in a predictable way.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Algo que se repite o cambia de una manera predecible.
vocabulary.example: 1 disc takes 1 move, 2 discs take 3, 3 discs take 7 — the moves follow a pattern.
vocabulary.visual: Circle, square, triangle, circle, square, triangle …
vocabulary.cloze: Objects or shapes repeated in a regular order form a ___.

examples.text: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 — each is double the last plus 1
examples.why: The change follows a rule you can predict.
Nothing lets you say what comes next.

vocabulary.definitionEs: Una regla que te dice cómo obtener el siguiente valor de un patrón a partir del anterior.
vocabulary.example: Double the number of steps and add 1 to find the steps for a tower with one more disc.
vocabulary.visual: 1 → 3 → 7 → 15: the rule is “double it and add 1”.
vocabulary.cloze: The rule for getting the next value from the one before is the ___ ___.

examples.why: It produces the next term from this one.
True, but it names no next value.

vocabulary.definitionEs: Decir lo que va a pasar antes de que pase, usando un patrón o el razonamiento.
vocabulary.example: The table let us predict that a five-disc tower takes 31 steps — without moving a single disc.
vocabulary.visual: The rule says a five-disc tower needs 31 steps — before moving a disc.
vocabulary.cloze: To say what will happen before it happens, using a pattern, is to ___.

examples.why: The pattern reaches a case you never played.

examples.text: Counting the moves after you finish

vocabulary.definition: To arrange information — often in a table — so patterns become easier to see.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Ordenar la información, muchas veces en una tabla, para que los patrones sean más fáciles de ver.
vocabulary.example: We can create a table of discs and steps to help us identify any patterns.
vocabulary.visual: Discs 1, 2, 3 in one column and steps 1, 3, 7 in the next.
vocabulary.cloze: To arrange information so patterns become easier to see is to ___ it.

examples.text: Putting the results in a table, in order
examples.why: Order is what makes the pattern visible.

examples.text: Writing results wherever there is room

launch.narrative: The Tower of Hanoi is a puzzle invented in 1883. It has three rods and a stack of discs, smallest on top to largest on the bottom. The number of discs can vary, but the number of rods does not — and hiding inside it is one of the prettiest patterns in mathematics.

conceptIntro.heading: Playing with math means playing with patterns
conceptIntro.intro: The objective is to move the whole stack of discs to another rod. The rules: move only one disc at a time, move only the top disc from a stack, and never place a larger disc on top of a smaller disc.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Algorithmic Thinking & Recursive Patterns. 1. Deconstruct complex multi-step problems into smaller, repeatable sub-tasks. 2. Trace patterns from simple cases to formulate general mathematical rules. 3. Verify algorithmic rules across edge cases and increasing problem sizes

iDo.title: Watch me imagine the solution first
lines: Before moving anything, I describe what the solved puzzle will look like: the discs in the same order — smallest on top to largest on bottom — but on a different rod.
Then I play the small cases: a one-disc tower takes 1 move, and a two-disc tower takes 3 moves.
A three-disc tower takes at least 7 moves. Small cases are how mathematicians play.
linesEs: Antes de mover nada, describo cómo se verá el rompecabezas resuelto: los discos en el mismo orden — el más pequeño arriba y el más grande abajo — pero en otra varilla.
Luego juego los casos pequeños: una torre de un disco toma 1 movimiento, y una de dos discos toma 3 movimientos.
Una torre de tres discos toma al menos 7 movimientos. Los casos pequeños son la forma en que juegan los matemáticos.

weDo.title: Let's organize the moves in a table
lines: Discs: 1, 2, 3 — Steps: 1, 3, 7. What is happening from each row to the next?
Double the number of steps and add 1: 1 doubled plus 1 is 3, and 3 doubled plus 1 is 7.
So 4 discs take 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps, and 5 discs take 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps.
The pattern just solved a puzzle we never touched.
linesEs: Discos: 1, 2, 3 — Pasos: 1, 3, 7. ¿Qué pasa de una fila a la siguiente?
Duplica el número de pasos y suma 1: 1 duplicado más 1 es 3, y 3 duplicado más 1 es 7.
Entonces 4 discos toman 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 pasos, y 5 discos toman 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 pasos.
El patrón acaba de resolver un rompecabezas que nunca tocamos.
weDo.titleEs: Organicemos los movimientos en una tabla

youDo.title: Now you try
lines: Use the pattern rule to predict how many steps a six-disc tower needs.
Then tell a partner: will the number of steps ALWAYS be odd? Why or why not?
linesEs: Usa la regla del patrón para predecir cuántos pasos necesita una torre de seis discos.
Luego dile a un compañero: ¿el número de pasos siempre será impar? ¿Por qué sí o por qué no?

interactiveVisual.label: Check the rule: double the steps, then add.

conceptIntro.headingEs: Jugar con las matemáticas es jugar con patrones
conceptIntro.introEs: El objetivo es mover toda la pila de discos a otra varilla. Las reglas: mueve solo un disco a la vez, mueve solo el disco de arriba de una pila, y nunca pongas un disco más grande encima de uno más pequeño.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Pensamiento algorítmico y patrones recursivos. 1. Descompón problemas complejos de varios pasos en subtareas más pequeñas y repetibles. 2. Sigue los patrones desde los casos simples para formular reglas matemáticas generales. 3. Verifica las reglas del algoritmo en casos extremos y con problemas cada vez más grandes

explore.label: Legal move or against the rules? Sort each Tower of Hanoi move.

cards.text: Move the top disc of a stack to an empty rod
Place a small disc on top of a larger disc
Move one disc at a time
Move the smallest disc back to the rod it came from earlier
Place a larger disc on top of a smaller disc
Move two discs together in one move
Pull out a disc from the middle of a stack
Add a fourth rod to make the puzzle easier

explore.instructions: The rules are the whole game: one disc at a time, only the top disc of a stack, and a larger disc can never sit on a smaller disc. After sorting, tell a partner which rule is hardest to obey when you actually play.

connect.scenario: You solved the small towers by hand: 1 disc takes 1 step, 2 discs take 3 steps, 3 discs take 7 steps. Now someone hands you a five-disc tower and asks for the fewest steps — but you do not have time to play it out.
connect.promptQuestion: How can a pattern help you imagine the solution?
connect.prompt: The pattern rule for the Tower of Hanoi is to ___ the number of steps for the smaller tower and ___ for each new disc. Applying this rule twice starting from 7 steps for a three-disc tower gives a five-disc tower a minimum of ___ steps.

check.stem: The table shows: 1 disc = 1 step, 2 discs = 3 steps, 3 discs = 7 steps. What is the pattern rule from one row to the next?
choices: Add 2 to the previous number of steps
Double the previous number of steps and add 1
Multiply the previous number of steps by 3
Add the disc number to the previous steps
check.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so the rule is double and add 1. Adding 2 matches 1→3 but fails on 3→5≠7, multiplying by 3 matches 1→3 but fails on 3→9≠7, and adding the disc number matches 1+2=3 but fails on 3+3=6≠7.

check.stem: Using the rule "double the steps and add 1," how many steps does a 4-disc tower take, starting from the 3-disc value of 7 steps?
check.explanation: 7 × 2 + 1 = 15. 8 comes from only adding 1 without doubling, 14 comes from only doubling without adding 1, and 21 comes from tripling instead of doubling.

check.stem: Continuing the pattern from 15 steps for a 4-disc tower, how many steps does a 5-disc tower take?
check.explanation: 15 × 2 + 1 = 31. 16 comes from only adding 1, 30 comes from only doubling, and 45 comes from tripling 15 instead of doubling and adding 1.

connect.modelAnswer: I would organize what I know in a table: 1 disc takes 1 step, 2 discs take 3, 3 discs take 7. The pattern rule is to double the number of steps and add 1 for each new disc. So 4 discs take 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps, and 5 discs take 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps. The pattern let me imagine the solution — a minimum of 31 steps — without ever touching the discs.

approaching.stem: What is the fewest number of moves needed to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
choices: 7 moves
3 moves
6 moves
9 moves
approaching.explanation: It takes at least 7 moves to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
choiceFeedback: 3 is the number of DISCS — moving each disc only once is impossible because of the size rule.
6 doubles the 3 discs but forgets the extra move — the pattern is double and add 1, so 3 discs need 7.
9 is 3 × 3, but the fewest-moves count follows the doubling pattern, not disc × disc.
hints: It is more than one move per disc.
A two-disc tower already takes 3 moves.
Double 3 and add 1.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el menor número de movimientos necesarios para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos?
approaching.explanationEs: Se necesitan al menos 7 movimientos para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos.
hintsEs: Es más de un movimiento por disco.
Una torre de dos discos ya toma 3 movimientos.
Duplica 3 y suma 1.

approaching.stem: Which move is against the rules of the Tower of Hanoi?
choices: Placing a larger disc on top of a smaller disc
Moving one disc at a time
Moving the top disc from a stack
Placing a smaller disc on top of a larger disc
approaching.explanation: A larger disc can never be on top of a smaller disc — that is the rule that makes the puzzle a puzzle.
choiceFeedback: One disc at a time is exactly what the rules require, not what they forbid.
You may only move the TOP disc of a stack — that move follows the rules.
Smaller on top of larger is the legal direction; it is the reverse that is banned.
hints: Two of these are the rules themselves.
Think about disc SIZES.
Which stacking order would crush a smaller disc?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál movimiento va contra las reglas de la Torre de Hanói?
approaching.explanationEs: Un disco más grande nunca puede estar sobre uno más pequeño — esa es la regla que hace que el rompecabezas sea un rompecabezas.
hintsEs: Dos de estas son las reglas mismas.
Piensa en los TAMAÑOS de los discos.
¿Cuál orden de apilado aplastaría un disco más pequeño?

approaching.stem: What will the solved puzzle look like?
choices: The discs in the same order — smallest on top to largest on bottom — but on a different rod
The discs in reverse order, largest on top
The discs spread out with one disc on each rod
The discs back on the starting rod in any order
approaching.explanation: The goal is to rebuild the whole stack, smallest to largest, on a different rod.
choiceFeedback: Largest on top would break the rule — a larger disc can never sit on a smaller one.
Spreading the discs out is a middle step, not the finished puzzle.
The stack must END on a different rod, and the size order is required, not optional.
hints: Imagine the ending before you start.
The stack looks just like the start.
Only its rod has changed.
approaching.explanationEs: La meta es reconstruir toda la pila, del más pequeño al más grande, en otra varilla.
hintsEs: Imagina el final antes de empezar.
La pila se ve igual que al inicio.
Solo cambió su varilla.

approaching.stem: How many moves does a one-disc tower take? A two-disc tower?
choices: 1 move and 3 moves
1 move and 2 moves
2 moves and 4 moves
1 move and 4 moves
approaching.explanation: You can solve a one-disc tower in 1 step and a two-disc tower in 3 steps.
choiceFeedback: 2 moves is not enough for two discs — the small disc must move aside, the large disc moves, then the small disc moves back on top: 3 moves.
One disc needs only 1 move — just lift it to another rod.
4 moves is one too many for two discs — the fewest is 3.
hints: Play the one-disc game in your head first.
For two discs: the small one has to get out of the way, and later get back on top.
Count those three separate moves.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuántos movimientos toma una torre de un disco? ¿Y una de dos discos?
approaching.explanationEs: Puedes resolver una torre de un disco en 1 paso y una de dos discos en 3 pasos.
hintsEs: Juega primero en tu mente el juego de un disco.
Para dos discos: el pequeño tiene que quitarse del camino y después volver arriba.
Cuenta esos tres movimientos por separado.

approaching.stem: The number of discs in a Tower of Hanoi puzzle can vary. What NEVER varies?
approaching.modelAnswer: The number of rods never varies — there are always three rods, no matter how many discs the puzzle uses.
approaching.stemEs: El número de discos en la Torre de Hanói puede variar. ¿Qué NUNCA varía?

approaching.stem: What does it mean to be playful with math? Use the Tower of Hanoi as your example.
approaching.modelAnswer: Being playful with math means treating a problem like a game — imagining what the solution will look like, trying small cases, and hunting for a pattern. With the Tower of Hanoi, I played the one-disc and two-disc towers first, and the pattern I found told me about towers I never played.
sentenceStems: With the Tower of Hanoi, I ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué significa ser juguetón con las matemáticas? Usa la Torre de Hanói como ejemplo.

approaching.instructions: Sort each move: is it allowed by the Tower of Hanoi rules, or against them?
approaching.instructionsEs: Clasifica cada movimiento: ¿lo permiten las reglas de la Torre de Hanói o va en contra de ellas?
approaching.label: Sort each move: legal or against the rules?
approaching.labelEs: Clasifica cada movimiento: ¿legal o contra las reglas?

categories.label: Legal move
items: Move the top disc of any stack
Place a small disc on a bigger disc
Move exactly one disc at a time
itemsEs: Mover el disco de arriba de cualquier pila
Colocar un disco pequeño sobre uno más grande
Mover exactamente un disco a la vez

categories.label: Against the rules
items: Place a big disc on a smaller disc
Pull a disc out from the middle of a stack
itemsEs: Mover dos discos a la vez
Colocar un disco grande sobre uno más pequeño
Sacar un disco de en medio de una pila

hints: Only the TOP disc of a stack can move, and only one at a time.
The size rule: smaller may rest on bigger, never the reverse.
hintsEs: Solo el disco de ARRIBA de una pila puede moverse, y solo uno a la vez.
La regla del tamaño: el pequeño puede descansar sobre el grande, nunca al revés.
approaching.explanation: The three legal moves are the whole rule set: take only a top disc, move one at a time, and rest smaller on bigger. The illegal moves each break exactly one rule — two at once, big on small, or grabbing from mid-stack. Every 2ⁿ − 1 solution is built from nothing but the legal three.
approaching.explanationEs: Los tres movimientos legales son todo el reglamento: tomar solo el disco de arriba, mover uno a la vez y apoyar el pequeño sobre el grande. Los ilegales rompen exactamente una regla cada uno: dos a la vez, grande sobre pequeño o sacar de en medio. Cada solución de 2ⁿ − 1 se construye solo con los tres legales.

onLevel.stem: The table shows 1 disc → 1 step, 2 discs → 3 steps, 3 discs → 7 steps. What is the pattern rule for the number of steps when you add one more disc?
choices: Double the number of steps and add 1
Add 2 to the number of steps
Add the number of discs to the steps
Multiply the number of steps by 3
onLevel.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so each new disc doubles the steps and adds 1.
choiceFeedback: Adding 2 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 + 2 = 5, and the table says 7.
Adding the discs fits 1 → 3 (1 + 2) but fails the next row: 3 + 3 = 6, and the table says 7.
Multiplying by 3 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 × 3 = 9, and the table says 7.
hints: Test each rule on BOTH jumps: 1 → 3 and 3 → 7.
Several rules pass the first jump; only one passes both.
What do you do to 3 to land exactly on 7?
onLevel.stemEs: La tabla muestra 1 disco → 1 paso, 2 discos → 3 pasos, 3 discos → 7 pasos. ¿Cuál es la regla del patrón para el número de pasos cuando agregas un disco más?
onLevel.explanationEs: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 y 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, así que cada disco nuevo duplica los pasos y suma 1.
hintsEs: Prueba cada regla en LOS DOS saltos: 1 → 3 y 3 → 7.
Varias reglas pasan el primer salto; solo una pasa los dos.
¿Qué le haces al 3 para caer exactamente en 7?

onLevel.stem: Use the pattern rule to complete the table: how many steps for a four-disc tower?
choices: 15 steps
14 steps
9 steps
28 steps
onLevel.explanation: A three-disc tower takes 7 steps, so a four-disc tower takes 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps.
choiceFeedback: 14 doubles the 7 steps but forgets to add 1.
9 adds 2 to 7 instead of doubling and adding 1.
28 multiplies 7 by 4 (the number of discs) instead of doubling once and adding 1.
hints: Start from the three-disc answer: 7 steps.
Apply the rule: double, then add 1.
onLevel.stemEs: Usa la regla del patrón para completar la tabla: ¿cuántos pasos para una torre de cuatro discos?
onLevel.explanationEs: Una torre de tres discos toma 7 pasos, así que una torre de cuatro discos toma 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 pasos.
hintsEs: Empieza con la respuesta de tres discos: 7 pasos.
Aplica la regla: duplica y luego suma 1.

onLevel.stem: What is the minimum number of steps to solve a FIVE-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
choices: 31 steps
15 steps
30 steps
35 steps
onLevel.explanation: A four-disc tower takes 15 steps, so a five-disc tower takes 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps.
choiceFeedback: 15 steps is the answer for FOUR discs — the fifth disc requires applying the rule once more.
30 doubles the 15 steps but forgets to add 1.
35 adds 5 discs × 4 to 15 — the rule is double and add 1, not add a multiple of the discs.
hints: You need the four-disc answer first: 15.
Apply the rule one more time.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el número mínimo de pasos para resolver la Torre de Hanói de CINCO discos?
onLevel.explanationEs: Una torre de cuatro discos toma 15 pasos, así que una torre de cinco discos toma 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 pasos.
hintsEs: Necesitas primero la respuesta de cuatro discos: 15.
Aplica la regla una vez más.

onLevel.stem: How can you ORGANIZE the information about discs and moves to help you see patterns?
onLevel.modelAnswer: I can create a table with one column for the number of discs and one for the number of steps: 1 and 1, 2 and 3, 3 and 7, 4 and 15, 5 and 31. With the numbers lined up in rows, I can compare each row to the next and spot the double-and-add-1 pattern.
sentenceStems: I can organize the information in a ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cómo puedes ORGANIZAR la información sobre discos y movimientos para ayudarte a ver patrones?

onLevel.stem: Why is finding a pattern MORE powerful than just solving the three-disc puzzle by hand?
choices: The pattern predicts the answer for towers you have never played, like five or six discs
The pattern lets you skip the rules of the puzzle
Patterns make the discs move by themselves
A pattern proves the puzzle is impossible
onLevel.explanation: The pattern told us a five-disc tower needs a minimum of 31 steps — without moving a single disc.
choiceFeedback: The rules always apply — the pattern predicts the move COUNT, it does not change what moves are legal.
You still make every move yourself; the pattern only tells you how many to expect.
The pattern shows the puzzle IS solvable at every size, and says how many steps it takes.
hints: What did the table tell us about the five-disc tower?
Did we ever play the five-disc tower by hand?
Prediction is the power.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Por qué encontrar un patrón es MÁS poderoso que solo resolver a mano el rompecabezas de tres discos?
onLevel.explanationEs: El patrón nos dijo que una torre de cinco discos necesita un mínimo de 31 pasos — sin mover ni un solo disco.
hintsEs: ¿Qué nos dijo la tabla sobre la torre de cinco discos?
¿Alguna vez jugamos a mano la torre de cinco discos?
Predecir es lo poderoso.

onLevel.stem: Before solving, the lesson asked you to DESCRIBE what the solution will look like. Why is imagining the ending a useful way to start a puzzle?
onLevel.modelAnswer: Imagining the ending gives me a target. Once I know the discs must end up smallest-on-top on a different rod, I can judge every move by whether it gets me closer to that picture. Math can help us imagine what might happen before it happens.
sentenceStems: Then each move can be judged by ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Antes de resolver, la lección te pidió DESCRIBIR cómo se verá la solución. ¿Por qué imaginar el final es una manera útil de empezar un rompecabezas?

onLevel.stem: Will the fewest number of steps for a Tower of Hanoi puzzle always be an ODD number?
choices: Yes — doubling any whole number gives an even number, and adding 1 makes it odd
No — every other tower size gives an even number of steps
Yes — but only because 7 happens to be odd
No — the steps alternate between odd and even
onLevel.explanation: Each answer comes from doubling the one before (always even) and adding 1 (always odd): 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 are all odd, and the rule guarantees the next one will be too.
choiceFeedback: Check the table: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 — no even number ever appears.
It is not luck about 7 — the double-and-add-1 rule FORCES every result to be odd, forever.
The list 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 never alternates — every entry is odd.
hints: Look at the whole list: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
What kind of number is 'double anything'?
What happens when you add 1 to an even number?
onLevel.stemEs: ¿El menor número de pasos de la Torre de Hanói siempre será un número IMPAR?
onLevel.explanationEs: Cada respuesta viene de duplicar la anterior (siempre par) y sumar 1 (siempre impar): 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 son todos impares, y la regla garantiza que el siguiente también lo será.
hintsEs: Mira toda la lista: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
¿Qué tipo de número es 'el doble de cualquier cosa'?
¿Qué pasa cuando le sumas 1 a un número par?

onLevel.label: Use the doubling pattern to complete the table of fewest moves.
onLevel.labelEs: Usa el patrón de duplicación para completar la tabla de movimientos mínimos.
hints: Each new disc means: solve the smaller tower, move the big disc, solve the smaller tower again.
That is why the rule is double-plus-one: two copies of the previous answer, plus one move for the biggest disc.
hintsEs: Cada disco nuevo significa: resolver la torre más pequeña, mover el disco grande y resolver la torre pequeña otra vez.
Por eso la regla es duplicar y sumar uno: dos copias de la respuesta anterior más un movimiento para el disco más grande.
onLevel.explanation: The recursion is the reason for the rule: to move n discs you solve n − 1 discs (7 moves), carry the biggest disc (1 move), and solve n − 1 again (7 moves) — so 4 discs need 15, 5 need 31, and 6 need 2 × 31 + 1 = 63. The pattern 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63 is one less than the doubling numbers 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.
onLevel.explanationEs: La recursión explica la regla: para mover n discos resuelves n − 1 discos (7 movimientos), llevas el disco más grande (1 movimiento) y resuelves n − 1 otra vez (7 movimientos); por eso 4 discos necesitan 15, 5 necesitan 31 y 6 necesitan 2 × 31 + 1 = 63. El patrón 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63 es uno menos que los números que se duplican: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.

extending.stem: A five-disc tower takes 31 steps. Using the pattern rule, how many steps would a SIX-disc tower take?
choices: 63 steps
62 steps
36 steps
32 steps
extending.explanation: Apply the rule to 31: double it and add 1, so 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 steps.
choiceFeedback: 62 doubles the 31 steps but forgets to add 1.
36 adds 5 to 31 — the rule doubles the steps rather than adding the disc count.
32 adds 1 to 31 but forgets to double first.
hints: The rule works from any row of the table.
Double, then add 1.
extending.stemEs: Una torre de cinco discos toma 31 pasos. Usando la regla del patrón, ¿cuántos pasos tomaría una torre de SEIS discos?
extending.explanationEs: Aplica la regla a 31: duplícalo y suma 1, así que 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 pasos.
hintsEs: La regla funciona desde cualquier fila de la tabla.
Duplica y luego suma 1.

extending.stem: Look at the table a different way: 1 disc → 1, 2 discs → 3, 3 discs → 7, 4 discs → 15, 5 discs → 31. Which describes the relationship between the number of discs and the number of steps?
choices: The steps are 1 less than a doubling pattern: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 each minus 1
The steps are the number of discs multiplied by itself
The steps are 6 times the number of discs, plus or minus 1
The steps are the two previous step counts added together
extending.explanation: 2 − 1 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, 8 − 1 = 7, 16 − 1 = 15, 32 − 1 = 31 — every entry is one less than the doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
choiceFeedback: Discs times itself gives 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 — that misses the table from the second row on.
6 times the discs gives 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 — even allowing plus or minus 1, that fails the first rows.
Adding previous entries gives 1 + 3 = 4 for the third row, but the table says 7.
hints: Write the doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 above the steps 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
Compare them row by row.
How far apart is each pair?
extending.stemEs: Mira la tabla de otra manera: 1 disco → 1, 2 discos → 3, 3 discos → 7, 4 discos → 15, 5 discos → 31. ¿Cuál describe la relación entre el número de discos y el número de pasos?
extending.explanationEs: 2 − 1 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, 8 − 1 = 7, 16 − 1 = 15, 32 − 1 = 31 — cada valor es uno menos que el patrón que duplica 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
hintsEs: Escribe el patrón que duplica 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 arriba de los pasos 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
Compáralos fila por fila.
¿Qué tan separado está cada par?

extending.stem: The 15 Puzzle is a sliding puzzle with 15 tiles in a frame 4 tiles high by 4 tiles wide. You arrange the tiles from 1 to 15 by sliding one tile at a time into the open space. Sometimes it is solvable and sometimes it is not. How would you make an argument about whether a particular 15 Puzzle is solvable, using what this lesson taught about being playful?
extending.modelAnswer: I would play the way we played the Tower of Hanoi: start with small cases and look for patterns. The frame is 4 × 4 = 16 spaces holding 15 tiles, so there is exactly one open space to slide into. I would try to solve it, keep track of which arrangements I can reach, and look for a pattern or relationship in the tile positions that separates the solvable starting setups from the impossible ones. If every attempt at a certain arrangement fails the same way, that repeated pattern becomes my evidence for arguing it is unsolvable.
sentenceStems: My argument would use the pattern ___ .
extending.stemEs: El Rompecabezas del 15 es un rompecabezas deslizante con 15 fichas en un marco de 4 fichas de alto por 4 de ancho. Ordenas las fichas del 1 al 15 deslizando una a la vez hacia el espacio vacío. A veces tiene solución y a veces no. ¿Cómo construirías un argumento sobre si un Rompecabezas del 15 en particular tiene solución, usando lo que esta lección enseñó sobre ser juguetón?

extending.stem: The summary says playing with math lets us think differently by looking for patterns AND by imagining ways to visualize a problem. Describe how you used BOTH of those with the Tower of Hanoi.
extending.modelAnswer: I used imagination first: before moving anything, I pictured the solved puzzle — the same stack, smallest on top, standing on a different rod. Then I used patterns: I organized the small cases in a table (1 disc → 1 step, 2 → 3, 3 → 7) and found the double-and-add-1 rule, which predicted 15 steps for four discs and 31 for five. Imagining gave me the target, and the pattern gave me the count — together they solved towers I never touched.
sentenceStems: I found the pattern ___ , which predicted ___ .
extending.stemEs: El resumen dice que jugar con las matemáticas nos permite pensar de otra manera al buscar patrones Y al imaginar formas de visualizar un problema. Describe cómo usaste AMBAS con la Torre de Hanói.

extending.label: Match each tower to the calculation that gives its fewest moves.
extending.labelEs: Empareja cada torre con el cálculo que da sus movimientos mínimos.

pairs.matchEs: Duplicar la respuesta de (n − 1) discos y sumar 1

hints: Each calculation reuses the answer for one disc fewer — find the chain.
The last card states the general rule; the other three are that rule applied.
hintsEs: Cada cálculo reutiliza la respuesta de un disco menos: encuentra la cadena.
La última tarjeta enuncia la regla general; las otras tres son esa regla aplicada.
extending.explanation: The chain 7 → 15 → 31 → 63 applies double-plus-one three times, and the fourth card names the general rule that generates the whole sequence. Recognizing a specific pattern AND its general statement as the same idea is the heart of algorithmic thinking in this lesson.
extending.explanationEs: La cadena 7 → 15 → 31 → 63 aplica duplicar-más-uno tres veces, y la cuarta tarjeta nombra la regla general que genera toda la secuencia. Reconocer que un patrón específico Y su enunciado general son la misma idea es el corazón del pensamiento algorítmico de esta lección.

practice.commonMistake: Doubling the previous number of steps but forgetting to add 1 — answering 14 instead of 15 for four discs, or 30 instead of 31 for five.

diagram.title: Fewest Moves in Tower of Hanoi
diagram.caption: Each bar doubles the one before it and adds 1: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. One more disc nearly doubles the work, so the bars grow far faster than the disc count.

exitTicket.stem: Which statement best shows what this lesson means by 'math is playful'?
choices: We play with math by imagining possible solutions and looking for patterns that help us think logically about puzzles
Math is playful only when there are no rules to follow
Puzzles like the Tower of Hanoi can only be solved by trial and error
Playing with math means guessing until something works
exitTicket.explanation: The summary names both moves: imagining different ways to visualize the problem, and looking for patterns or relationships that help us think logically.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It names imagination AND patterns.
Which option keeps both?

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explanation: A square folds onto itself along both diagonals and both midlines — 4 lines in all.

questions.stem: A shape has bilateral symmetry. This means…
choices: one line splits it into two mirror halves
it has four equal sides
it can be turned in a circle
it has no straight edges
questions.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means a single line divides the shape into halves that mirror each other.

questions.stem: Which capital letter has a vertical line of symmetry?
choices: A
R
P
F
questions.explanation: A folds onto itself along a vertical line down its middle. R, P and F do not.

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
questions.explanation: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry — one through each pair of opposite vertices and each pair of opposite sides.

Something that repeats or changes in a predictable way
To say what will happen before it happens

steps: 1. Deconstruct complex multi-step problems into smaller, repeatable sub-tasks
2. Trace patterns from simple cases to formulate general mathematical rules
3. Verify algorithmic rules across edge cases and increasing problem sizes
